draft.title: The Delphi Murders: What the Case File Shows
draft.excerpt: A secret smartphone recording captured a killer in Delphi, Indiana, but it took over five years and a misfiled tip to close the case.
body: On February 13, 2017, a 14-year-old girl in Delphi, Indiana, saw a man walking toward her on a remote railway bridge. She had the presence of mind to pull out her smartphone and hit record. That secret recording captured a grainy image of a man in a dark jacket and jeans, and audio of him saying three words: "Down the hill."

For over five years, that video was the center of the Delphi murders investigation. The public analyzed the footage of the man they called "Bridge Guy," while investigators searched for a break. You've probably heard the headline version of this story. The bodies of 14-year-old Liberty Rose "Libby" Lynn German and 13-year-old Abigail "Abby" Joyce Williams were found the next day, and the case captivated the country.

I went back through the case file. The biggest break did not come from a dramatic undercover sting. It came from a retired child protective service investigator volunteering as a file clerk. She found a misfiled tip from 2017. Let's unpack what the evidence actually shows.
## The Monon High Bridge

At 1:30 p.m. on February 13, 2017, Liberty Rose "Libby" Lynn German and Abigail "Abby" Joyce Williams were dropped off by Kelsi German, Liberty German's older sister. They were at County Road 300 North, east of the Hoosier Heartland Highway in Delphi, Indiana. They planned to spend their day off from school hiking on the Monon High Bridge over Deer Creek.

The bridge sits among woodland in remote Deer Creek Township. At 2:07 p.m., Liberty German used social media to post a photo of Abigail Williams walking across the bridge. That was the last time anyone heard from them. They were supposed to meet Liberty German's father at 3:15 p.m., but they never showed up.

The families searched the area themselves before calling the police. At 5:30 p.m., the girls were officially reported missing. Authorities searching the Delphi Historic Trails did not initially suspect foul play. That changed around noon the following day. The bodies of both girls were discovered on the north bank of Deer Creek, about 0.5 miles east of the abandoned Monon High Bridge.
## The Smartphone Evidence

Police kept the details of the crime scene quiet. On February 15, 2017, the Indiana State Police began circulating a still image. It showed a white male with his hands in his pockets and his head down, walking on the rail bridge toward the girls. Days later, this "Bridge Guy" was named the prime suspect in the double homicide.

On February 22, law enforcement held a press conference. They released a muffled audio recording of the suspect saying, "Down the hill." Officials credited Liberty German's smartphone for both the audio and the images. They called her a hero for having the fortitude to secretly record the exchange.

Police indicated they had secured additional evidence from the phone. They refused to release further details, stating they did not want to compromise any future trial. A reward was set at US$41,000. Over the next few years, police released composite sketches and asked for help identifying the driver of a vehicle parked near the former Child Services office. But the case went cold.
## The Misfiled Tip

In September 2022, a volunteer file clerk named Kathy Shank changed the course of the investigation. Kathy Shank had worked for 40 years as a child protective service investigator before retiring. She was spending hours filing and organizing thousands of tips for the Carroll County Sheriff's office.

She found a file folder that was out of place. It was marked "cleared." The sheet inside showed that three days after the murders, a man had self-reported being on the trails between 1:30 p.m. and 3:30 p.m. on the day of the crime. The self-reporter noted that he saw three girls. The name on the file was recorded incorrectly as "Richard Allen Whiteman."

The clerk realized the names were likely transposed, as the man lived on Whiteman Drive. She wrote a lead sheet and brought Richard Matthew Allen to the attention of investigators. Carroll County Sheriff Tony Liggett later stated that the tip fell through the cracks in 2017. On October 26, 2022, Richard Matthew Allen was taken into custody.
## What the Affidavit Revealed

On October 31, 2022, the Indiana State Police announced that Richard Matthew Allen was charged with two counts of murder. He pled not guilty. A month later, Judge Frances Gull unsealed the probable cause affidavit. The redacted document outlined exactly what investigators found.

The affidavit revealed that video footage from Liberty German's phone showed one of the victims mentioning a "gun" as a man in a dark jacket and jeans approached them. Investigators stated they believed Richard Matthew Allen was the man in the video. The document also noted that an unspent .40-caliber round was found less than two feet from one victim's body, lying between the two girls.

Police analysis later determined that the unspent round was cycled through a Sig Sauer Model P226 owned by Richard Matthew Allen. The affidavit included witness statements. One witness saw a man walking away from the bridge wearing a blue jacket and blue jeans, noting he was muddy and bloody. Another witness reported a car parked oddly, as if to hide its license plate. Investigators said this matched a vehicle Richard Matthew Allen owned in 2017.
## The Man in Plain Sight

Delphi, Indiana, is a small city. Platted in 1828 and named after the ancient city in Greece, it is the county seat of Carroll County. According to the 2020 census, it has a population of 2,961 people and is 100 percent rural. Investigators had stated they believed the suspect might be hiding in plain sight.

Richard Matthew Allen was born in September 1972 and grew up in Mexico, Indiana. He graduated from North Miami Middle/High School in 1991, where he played football and participated in track and field. He studied accounting at Ivy Tech Community College and had short stints in the U.S. Army and National Guard.

In December 2006, he moved to Delphi. He worked as a store manager at a Logansport Walmart from 2003 until 2013. Later, he worked at CVS Pharmacy stores in neighboring Peru and in Delphi, receiving his pharmacy technician license in February 2018. His wife, Kathy Allen, later said he was on the couch when she got home the evening of February 13, 2017. When she saw the news that two girls were missing, she said he seemed surprised.
## The Trial of Richard Matthew Allen

The trial began on October 18, 2024, in Delphi. Prosecutor Nick McLeland laid out a grim scene. Prosecutors stated both girls had their throats cut. Abigail Williams was found fully clothed in Liberty German's clothing, while Liberty German was discovered nude. A police firearms examiner testified about the "quality and quantity of marks" linking the unspent bullet to Richard Matthew Allen's gun.

The prosecution focused heavily on confessions. Prosecutors told the jury that Richard Matthew Allen admitted to the murders more than 60 times while incarcerated. He confessed to his wife, his mother, family members, the prison warden, other inmates, and the psychologist treating him. A State Police Master Trooper testified that he listened to over 700 prison phone calls and concluded that the voice of the "Bridge Guy" was Richard Matthew Allen.

A clinical psychologist for the Indiana Department of Corrections Behavioral Health testified for the defense. She stated Richard Matthew Allen was diagnosed with a serious mental illness. According to her testimony, he told her he originally planned to sexually assault the victims but ran away when he saw a van nearby, then cut the girls' throats and covered their bodies with sticks.

Defense attorney Andrew Baldwin argued that the confessions were caused by a mental health crisis resulting from 13 months in solitary confinement. The defense also hired a neuropsychologist who testified about Richard Matthew Allen's severe depression and anxiety. In previous motions, the defense claimed the murders were actually committed by Odinists, members of a Norse pagan religion, as part of a ritual sacrifice. They also noted a hair found on Abigail Williams's hand was not a match for Richard Matthew Allen.
## The Verdict and Where It Stands

The jury was sequestered during the trial. On November 7, 2024, they began deliberations. Four days later, on November 11, 2024, Richard Matthew Allen was convicted on all counts. On December 20, 2024, Judge Frances Gull sentenced him to 65 years for the murder of Liberty German and 65 years for the murder of Abigail Williams. The sentences run consecutively, totaling 130 years in prison.

Richard Matthew Allen was transported to Westville Correctional Facility, then Pendleton Correctional Facility. On July 18, 2025, he was transferred to the Lexington Assessment and Reception Center in Oklahoma under an interstate compact agreement. On April 9, 2025, interrogation videos and eight phone conversations featuring his confessions to his wife and mother were released to the public.

The community of Delphi continues to honor the victims. Homeowners across central Indiana installed orange porch lights to commemorate the girls. The L & A Park Foundation developed the Abby and Libby Memorial Park a mile north of Delphi. The Delphi Community Middle School renamed its library the Abby and Libby Memorial Library.
The legal process has concluded, and the evidence is part of the public record. Read the file. Form your own conclusion.
